Early life stages of Jarbua terapon are characterised by a very small initial mass, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing just 0.000092 grams [Wwb = 0.000092 grams]. This minute body size, derived from an egg diameter of approximately 560 micrometres, reflects the pelagic spawning strategy common among teraponids, where numerous small eggs are released into the water column. Following a brief endotrophic phase during which the larva relies entirely on its yolk reserves, the onset of exogenous feeding occurs after the mouth opens and the yolk sac is largely resorbed. The larval period involves a planktonic existence, during which the growing fish undergoes flexion and subsequent metamorphosis before transitioning to a benthic juvenile habit. This developmental trajectory, typical of many teleosts that broadcast spawn, imposes high initial mortality but allows for the production of a large number of offspring per spawning event, a trait that becomes especially relevant under the warm thermal regime typically encountered in tropical coastal waters.

Juveniles of Terapon jarbua grow rapidly during their first year of life, and the attainment of sexual maturity is linked to a specific body size. Field studies indicate that puberty is reached at a standard length of approximately 13 centimetres [Lp = approximately 13 centimetres], a milestone typically achieved by the end of the first year or the beginning of the second year of life. This length corresponds to a wet body mass of roughly 36.6 grams [Wwp = roughly 36.6 grams] when estimated from the length-weight relationship characteristic of the species. The transition to reproductive maturity marks a significant shift in life history allocation, as the fish begins to divert resources from purely somatic growth toward gamete production. Individuals at this size are considered to have completed the sub-adult phase and entered the breeding population, though their reproductive contribution may be lower than that of larger, more experienced adults.

At a stable water temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C], the maximum reproductive output observed in this species is considerable. This high reproductive potential is typical of fishes that inhabit dynamic coastal environments, where unpredictable conditions favour the production of many small offspring over the investment in a few large ones. The pelagic eggs and larvae are dispersed widely by currents, a strategy that reduces competition among siblings but exposes them to high rates of planktonic predation. Such a life history pattern underscores the species' adaptation to variable estuarine and inshore habitats.

The ultimate size that Jarbua terapon can achieve under favourable conditions has been documented from large adult specimens. The maximum recorded standard length for this species is 36 centimetres [Li = 36 centimetres], and the corresponding ultimate wet body mass is approximately 794 grams [Wwi = approximately 794 grams], derived from the length-weight power function commonly applied to teraponid fishes. Achieving this size requires several years of sustained growth and access to ample food resources, typically in productive estuarine or coastal environments. Large adults occupy a higher trophic position and are capable of consuming a wider range of prey, including smaller fishes and larger crustaceans. Their size also confers a degree of protection from gape-limited predators, allowing these individuals to contribute to the population over multiple breeding seasons. Comparisons with smaller-bodied related species highlight the relatively large maximum size attained by Terapon jarbua within its genus.

Lifespan data for Terapon jarbua indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 3,285 days [am = approximately 3,285 days] when measured under controlled conditions at a temperature of 23.7 °C [T = 23.7 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to about nine years, is notable among smaller estuarine fishes and allows for repeated spawning events over many years, a classic iteroparous strategy. The species' ability to survive for nearly a decade is likely linked to its relatively large ultimate body size and its position as a mid-level predator in coastal food webs, which reduces natural mortality rates compared to smaller, short-lived forage fishes. Older individuals represent a small fraction of the population but contribute disproportionately to lifetime fecundity, as their larger body size enables greater egg production per spawning event. Their persistence in the environment also provides valuable demographic stability to the population.
